sections.h:
We must always go where the greatest need requires it.

My voice: Finish quickly with that farmstead and go to the one you left a little while ago. V—. 109.

Running, I met a good shepherd whom at other times I had made use of to set right certain workers who, horribly tempted, would have taken flight. I begged him to follow me and to be willing, this time too, to take care of certain workers who are undisciplined. He looked at me and said to me: If you please, it is a farmstead where they all do as they like.

— Well — I answered him — must we not always go where the greatest need requires it?

Frankly he answered me: I do not feel up to it!

Oh! how embarrassed I felt! I kept thinking to myself: certainly he knows something terrible about it. And so, silent, I ran on without having given him an answer. He interrupts my silence and, in a charitable manner, tells me that he feels he cannot say no, but that he feels ready to follow me and lend his work.

And so along the way we spoke much of the great work of divine Providence, especially in this field so dear to Him. I do not know who will be able to understand better by reading these mute phrases, rather than by having described vividly what this poor slave was going through within herself. I felt weariness and did not want him to notice it; but the Lord permitted that this good shepherd’s strength should fail him, and he said to me:

— I cannot go on any longer; I must stop. He looked at me, and then said:

— What do you intend to do?

I answered:

— To continue my way: I shall wait for you at the farmhouse.

Having arrived at a convent, he stopped; and I, having entered for a few moments into the temple of my God, begged Him to give me strength, because I lacked it and could no longer walk. After a few moments, my voice:

— You have all that you need: run!

The devil compelled to light her road.

I set out on my way. Night was approaching, fear was already making itself felt, but I had strength like a giant. It was necessary to walk, but I kept repeating: I am afraid, my Teacher, my dear Lord! Ah! send me my angel! But I saw nothing. I prayed to the souls in purgatory, even those who had promised to come in my every need: nothing! My angel, where are you? I am afraid! A voice, but as if it remained in the air:

— I am with you!

— No! — I said loudly — I need to see you.

Meanwhile I hear a loud cackling of laughter: who can it be? I said loudly: Michael the Archangel, come! An ugly old man came forward, so horrid…; he was cackling with laughter. The fire that came out of his eyes let me see him clearly; his hair stood on end and he made grimaces.

— Away! I said to him.

He came forward to me. I said:

— Away, horrid beast!

He did not answer me. I saw that it was the one who had seduced a worker.

Ugly monster, away, and leave me in peace!

This ugly one became furious and tried to hurl himself at me to beat me hard.

— Halt, in the name of God! go to your chains.

He made such a loud din that it could be likened to one of the strongest thunderclaps. I thought it was all over and that he would no longer be permitted to come out: whereas a few steps on, there he is again.

— You are in the dark! — he said to me — with this stick I want to finish you.

Between the fear of the night and a certain sorrow at seeing myself alone, and with so much calling now one, now another to come with me, I gave a laugh of disdain at him and said to him mockingly:

— Buffoon, withdraw! Set fire to the stick; so it will burn and you will give me light along the road.

Truly that stick catches fire: it is a real torch.

— Take it and go before me!

He did not want to, and he made a thousand antics and grimaces of every kind: — No!

— Quick, take the stick and give light! obey me at once!

The fierce lion becomes my servant: he takes the torch and sets off; he gives me light. And when there were large stones on which I might stumble, he stopped so that I could see them. For a good two hours we walked in this way; when from afar the sound of a small bell was heard: I understood it to be that of the dwelling of the workers, ringing the rising. He turned toward me as if he wanted to throw that torch at me. But I at once ordered him to put it out and go back to where he had come from. He made some little grimace and then took his extinguished stick and disappeared.

As I was drawing near to enter the farmstead, a fit of laughter seized me so that I did not dare to go in, at the thought that that ugly one had been forced to give me light. It ceased. I went in without saying anything else and at once went, together with the others, to the little oratory.

Oh! how I felt refreshed to be at last tranquil and out of all danger! Oh! but having fed on my treasure, I poured out my heart, telling Him all that had happened to me. My voice:

— I have always been with you. I willed that even the devils should be obedient to you. Do you see (how out of place) your fear is?

— But — I added — what am I to do if fear seizes me? You know well that the mere thought of meeting men takes from me every faculty of being able to reason. If you do not take this fear from me, I shall always fall back into crying out and trembling. This fear takes possession of me and on every side I seem to see people. Forgive me, my God, have pity on my too great weakness!

My voice:

— Do not be distressed: all will pass.

How tranquil I remained!

Sweet Love! I have served you badly by mistaking the path!

Thus resigned, I ran on; but a deep sadness held me bound: all my mental faculties tied up, I was like a senseless person who walks, does not know where, and does not even understand that she is tired, a real donkey that goes on and on as long as its legs hold it up and then throws itself on the ground. So it happened to this slave of yours. Roused by weariness, I noticed that I was in a wood thick with trees: a sepulchral silence! My God, where am I? who led me here? My voice:

— Your carelessness!

How ever, without noticing it, do I find myself in so terrible a labyrinth? My God, pity! Ah! my Master, my Lord, mercy for my failing! And I repeated to myself: so I have been careless! Alas, what have I done? I threw myself on the ground among those plants: My Lord! I deserve nothing but to be devoured by wild beasts. I understand it: I deserve neither mercy nor forgiveness; let the vipers of this frightful wood devour me and I, resigned, will undergo the penalty. Oh! whatever have I done? And that melancholy, which always leads me, I felt it destroying me. Oh! I offended you, sweet Love! So badly have I served you by mistaking the path, and here I am! I took hold of certain big thorn branches and with all my strength I beat this donkey, because through its fault I had committed such carelessness; and I wept bitterly. A light all of a sudden (appears to me) and I feel myself seized by the arm and told: — Enough!

Oh! my angel! Prostrate, with joined hands, which were bloodied, I told him, weeping, that I had committed that carelessness and that certainly my Lord had been displeased by it and that I deserved nothing but to be devoured by the beasts.

He looked at me and, smiling, raised me up.

— Ah! why, my dear guide, did you permit me to stray from the path?

He answered me nothing. He looked at my hands and at the ground where the blood was, and then said to me: — This had to be shed for the good of certain fields that you will have to set in order. Dry your tears and come with me.

He took me by the hand and led me out of that wood. A beautiful light lit up my path, and it was brighter than the day itself.

— Do not leave me! — I said to him every minute; and I held his hand tight — But tell me truly: is my Lord no longer displeased with me?

— No: very dear to Him are your protestations, your anxieties and fears.

— But I suffer greatly! it is the torment of death!

— All is acceptable to Him and He takes pleasure in it.

Having said this, he pressed my hand, and disappeared.

A portion of her labors offered for the souls in purgatory.

Oh! — I exclaimed loudly — here I am alone! and where am I to go? My voice:

— Follow the light that guides you!

Already I felt myself fainting, but I did not want to stop, because the light pointed the way thus. Meanwhile it seemed to me from moment to moment that I would fall to the ground, and I prayed my Lord to send me my angel, because I felt myself fainting. And behold, the light no longer marks the path, but gathers all around me; I stop and it surrounds me as if it had enclosed me within itself. I was near a pretty stone. I sat down; I felt myself strengthened, I was gathering a little strength; but the long fast, the weariness, all that I had gone through (kept me exhausted).

I was praying and waiting for what I do not know: human refreshment certainly could not be had; but I do not know. I knew nothing, neither what to think nor how I should hope for comfort. Wrapped in that light and seated, I prayed. From the light itself came forth a graceful hand with a glass, and a voice that said to me: — Drink and you will be satisfied.

I drank. The light opened again and marked the path. And I, with a superhuman strength, ran. Meanwhile I began a little to perceive that it would soon be dawn. My mind went over all that had happened. A poor soul, who a few hours before had passed into eternity, was whispering to me to have prayers. So I thought to satisfy her desire; I would have wished other signs from her, but in vain.

— But why do you always trouble me to have from me… — so the sentence remained suspended, because my voice (interrupted me):

— What you desire you shall have, but there is still time.

She prays. Oh! dear soul, dear to God, blessed by my Lord for ever! But other souls present themselves to me in an attitude of supplication. Oh! dear friends, what can I do for you? I am a poor slave and worse: yes, for every now and then I serve my Master badly. I still feel the sorrow of a negligence committed: I was running carelessly, and where did I find myself? This conversation was held along my way.

— And now, dear friends, you see: I must walk, but I do not know either where or how I shall find a place to stop.

One answered me:

— It is very long, but it is very dear to God. Ah! offer for us a portion of these labors, so that we may soon be freed from so many pains.

I answered at once:

— Not a portion, but all this little bit that I am walking!

Oh! I hear a deep voice:

— And for me nothing? I have been condemned to darkness for so many years, and only from you can I have light.

My God! this voice is not new to me. Oh! that soul!… Ah! that I might see her. Here she is: how she suffered! And what was to be done? The labor of that journey was offered for those; I felt deep sorrow at not being able to give this one relief at once. Oh! the charity of the just soul! Both the souls I wished to benefit come readily before me:

— Your suffering is too great; it is just that that soul should have a portion of what you wished to do for us and be a sharer in the offering: very willingly we yield the right to it.

— Oh charity! Thank you, dear friends! and I promise you that I will redouble my care until I have the good fortune to see you in the heavenly homeland.

Oh! how I felt true consolation in it!

— Well, you are burning to be able soon to arrive at enjoying Him who forms for me all my longing, my only treasure, most sweet Master. Believe me, just like you I feel the sorrow and pain you feel, an inconceivable ardor to arrive there. Oh! when you have arrived at my God, tell Him that I desire soon what I have been asking Him for so long. Ah! speak to Him of me, and then remember to come.

They come near me, and one says to me:

— For me there will still be much; I suffer greatly: look at my pains!

Alas! a trembling seized me… Oh most merciful Savior! tell me what you want me to do for this poor soul: I offer myself to you to pay for her pains. My voice:

— Only in part do I permit it to you, because the journey is long and you will have to suffer worse than what you are suffering now on arrival. I was agitated; but the sight of those pains stood before me and (I had) a lively desire to relieve her. Well then, my Lord, even if only in part, but at least she will be relieved.

Great sufferings for the souls in purgatory — Help received from one of them.

Meanwhile I ran. Alas! crashes, howls…: I felt myself go all icy. Where do they come from? I saw nothing, although it was full noon. They grew ever louder. I felt myself fainting from fright. A rolling of stones…, the sky grew dark, thunder, lightning, a wind so violent that it tore off branches and threw them in my face; the stones were in the air like feathers, and yet they fell on me now on my face, now on my shoulders; I felt a strong pain on every side. There was no escape whereby to shelter; worse if I tried to lean against a large tree: this too, shaking its great branches, came to strike me.

I am lost! the pain in my poor head is terrible. Pity, my God! My angel, come to my aid! I feel myself dying. Certain beasts never seen before come out and fasten onto me, giving me such fierce bites that my strength fails me. Thrown to the ground, I fainted from the bites of these beasts; I had become swollen from them. Stretched on that ground soaked with water, I no longer understood anything; having lost my senses, I lay in that horrible position half-alive, and the beasts went on with their work. I say: went on, because, oh! I had them on me even when I came to. A strong voice roused me, saying to me: — Enough!

Alas! Alone! My God, ah! come to give me help. Parched with thirst, my throat dry, I looked at myself: I was all bloodied; and still those beasts went on biting me. I wept bitterly. So must I die under these bites? Go away, ugly beasts. And I see that, as I say this, they really do go away. Oh! are these diabolical insects? Away, ugly animals! get away from me! And they leave me.

Oh! — I said to myself — why did it not come to my mind before? The rain had stopped, the sky had become clear, and I felt almost completely healed of those bites, but exhausted, parched, and no longer frozen, but as if I had been in a furnace, so much did I feel myself burning; in breathing it seemed to me that flames came out of my mouth, so great was the heat. But, my God! night is advancing and I have no strength to rise. By now the fright is so great that I do not even dare to turn my gaze elsewhere. So I am abandoned! Ah! have pity on me!

— You wanted it! And consider that this is only one portion of what that soul suffers for whom you offered yourself.

I hear the approach of something I know not what and, between fear and hope that it might be my angel, I was panting. I was not mistaken: it was he.

— Enough! — he said to me — From now on you will never again make any offering: only prayers are you permitted to make for the souls in purgatory.

— For pity’s sake, do not leave me! It is night and I am afraid; I have no more strength, I am parched with thirst!

He takes me by the hand and brings to my lips something I know not what, which I had never tasted. As soon as I had drunk what (was contained) in this small but very graceful vessel, I felt full of strength, healthy and robust as before, and even more. What a wonder! And with a certain fear that he might go away, I kept repeating to him: — Do not leave me! it is night!

I hear that another creature is approaching, and behold, my angel has gone. Who was she? The soul for whom I had suffered so much comes near me, thanking me with such reassuring ways of her eternal gratitude that it moved me and I wept. She went on:

— Do not weep; great reward you will have for it from God too. Meanwhile I have the good fortune to be able to stay with you, keeping you company as far as your dwelling. And yet this is a great relief: for everything you will be rewarded.

— How so? — I said to her — It is I who must thank you for your company, for I am so afraid of the night.

Continuing still, I:

— You tell me that you are accompanying me as far as my destination: so you know where it is and what it is like, whether near or far?

She gave a great sigh, and then said:

— Yes, I know!

I added:

— But your sadness, your long sigh, makes me think that there is great evil there, or else a place of torments.

She answered me:

— Unfortunately, where you are going there are only cruel people: they have taken good workers from a field of the Lord and would like to seduce them; and, under the mantle of holiness, they try to carry out other subterfuges, because they would want them for their own fields, which have only the perfume of vainglory, ground where nothing good will ever grow and only couch grass will eat away all the other good plants: they will never have wheat. The more they try to steal good workers, the more barren their field will become; the fire of their ambition will always destroy every new plant whatever; and soon everything will be scattered. It will come into your power, and with good and wise workers you will make of it a delightful field for the Lord.

— But!… — and she stops with a long sigh.

— Ah! for pity’s sake, go on and tell me what I must do.

— I cannot! — she answers me.

— For charity’s sake, tell me what there is in that field?

— The charity done to me will spare you a portion of pains. I cannot add anything else, and I beg you not to insist.

I fell silent, but in my mind I kept reasoning, and the more I tried to guess, the more confused I found myself; and this poor soul looked at me with an air of compassion. A few more steps, and behold, she said to me: — My task is finished. And she left me.

Lively dispute with an old shepherd over the theft of a runaway worker.

I saw again in the distance a group of people who seemed to be fighting, but because of the great distance there was between us I could not distinguish well; but as I ran I began to hear certain shrieks: whatever has happened to those people? who were they? A good worker who was in despair because two of her workers were missing, and she was quarreling with an old shepherd because she was convinced that it was he who had led them off to another field. I quieted her at once and, turning to the good shepherd, I begged him that, if this were so, he would have the goodness to say so, for I would very willingly yield them to him, because I desire to help everyone, even the fields of others.

He flies into a rage and raises his stick to strike me. I dodged and felt like laughing. I said to him:

— Why such fury? If it is not true, we do not wish to blame you for anything because of it.

And I knelt down asking his pardon. But not even this availed. Who ever is this shepherd, so irritated?

— Although you will not accept my apologies, I still ask your pardon for whatever the poor overseer may have committed; but you must also forgive her sorrow, since the poor dear must render an account of it to the Lord, our Master.

Having said this, he seemed to calm down and told me to rise; but always in a rude manner. I was about to take my leave when I hear someone running and calling me loudly. I turned: it was one of those two. He turns flame-red in the face, and this poor dear throws herself on my neck and, weeping, (says to me):

— Why did you not arrive sooner?

I at once asked her about the other. She said to me:

— This old man carried us both away, leading us into an enclosed field, where there are certain old workers who, if you could see them, grumble continually. They wanted by force to make us put on certain bands around our heads; and then I, on seeing this, shrieked so loudly: I want my guide! And they had to let me run away.

He, enraged, wanted to strike us. I placed myself before him:

— Stop that stick! And if you were not a shepherd, I would make you feel it on your back!

He fell dumb and left me, saying to me:

— We shall see each other again!

— I beg you never again to return to the fields of the Lord! Send me my other worker.

And yet the two, that is, the overseer together with the one who arrived, helped me. As soon as the shepherd was gone, she burst into a flood of tears. She told me how it had gone: that he had made her a thousand promises, that those old women needed someone to take care of their field, and so they would accept us as overseers, and all of them would be subordinate. When it was quite otherwise: at his mere presence, what a whispering arose! they shrieked: We are the mistresses! And then they quarreled among themselves, saying that these were the intrigues of certain ones with the old shepherd.

— And that poor dear who remained there?

She answered:

— Oh! she certainly will not remain there. Meanwhile I was studying the means of being able to get her out. But on entering the farmstead, I found a little note, which she had lost, in which she told another companion of hers that going into that field was a means of then leaving them, and that they should wait for her. What pain I felt at it!

Meanwhile, tired as I was, I tried to have myself led to where my Lord was; and at the foot of His altar it seemed to me that I could find rest; but the poor workers, together with the overseer, after a long stay came to call me, begging me to be willing to go with them to take food. But I felt myself strengthened by my Lord and wanted nothing; but I had to yield to their insistence. So I set off to where the food was prepared.

While (there was) silence, and only the voice was heard of one who was reading, terrible fists were heard knocking loudly at the door of the farmstead. One went to see and came back frightened: it was the old shepherd, who was looking for the worker who had remained there, saying that she had gone off and was certainly with us. He wanted to be given back a sum that he had given her and other things of value which she had carried off from that field. I felt like laughing, because I was thinking of those old women: what an uproar they must have made! And I did not bother to give an answer to the one who was asking me what she should say to the old man. I rose and opened to him myself. Once he had come in, he turned his head here and there like a fury:

— Where is that thief?

— Whom are you looking for, if you please? — I say to him.

He flies into a rage and wanted to beat me by force; but I seized his stick:

— Gently with the threats! Silence: let us reason without uproar. The worker did not come here, and I assure you of it in truth. Let this suffice. I can only, out of charity, give you some clarification.

He begins to relate hurriedly what she had carried off from him; among the many things there were certain little devotional objects of an old woman who was very attached to them. Oh! — I thought to myself — what a terrible detachment! And then he: — Even my cloak!

— Poor man! — I said to him — really? I am sorry for it; but he who cheats, says the proverb, ends up cheated.

He was so agitated and confused that he understood little. I thought it well to console him and gave him the note found on the floor in the farmstead; he read it and then struck his forehead:

— Oh! it is done! Certainly we shall have nothing more. Where are these people?

— I do not know — I added.

He stays a moment lost in thought.

— Oh! — he exclaims at last — you must make it all good to us — he says to me in a resolute tone.

Laughing, I said to him:

— Of what? of the goods and money that she carried off? Oh! that is a fine one! — I added.

There followed a squabble so curious that every now and then a laugh escaped me. But at last he said:

— I shall have recourse to the law!

And so it happened. After a few hours he came back with two guards and before them accused me of having taken so much money from those poor old women, leaving them all in desolation, and that I must give it back. I let him speak at length, and then, turning to the judge, I said to him: — How can this be?

And I told him what had happened; but the shepherd argued his case, saying that this worker had previously been with us and that certainly she must have done as the first runaway did, and must have come to us, bringing the money. Turning to the judge, I said to him: — Can this be?

He answered me:

— It can be believed with every ease.

— Oh! — I exclaimed — this is a real insult to these poor dears.

And as proof that she had not come, I showed him the note. They remained (astonished) and, turning round, they said: — We have nothing more to do here.

But he insisted.

— Oh! — said I — Let us have done with it! otherwise you will have to pay us for the outrage you did us by coming stealthily to take our workers!

Meanwhile the old women, with a world of chatter, had in their own way made known what had happened to the superior of the diocese, and at that moment there reached me from him a very sharp note telling me to come to him. Well then, with resignation, I showed the note to the shepherd, who remained confused, one could see it, and begged me to let him go himself, for he would set everything right.

— No! It is I who am summoned, not you!

And in a flash, running, I went to the feet of the excellent shepherd. At once he scolded me, reproaching me for having made those poor old women suffer so much, and saying that it was right that I should give it back to them. I let him speak at length and then, with all humility, I asked him whether he would permit me to tell him the true story, and then I would submit to his justice. With an indifferent mind, without troubling myself too much about it and attaching no importance to it, I told him the facts. When I had finished, he said to me:

— How have you borne so much without making an uproar, and not even complaints; and I too, because of them, scolded you…: I beg you to forgive me.

And he made me a thousand apologies, assuring me that he would do me justice. Having returned to the farmstead, my voice:

— It is not over yet.

So it was: the old women, seeing themselves lost and that there was no more hope for them with the good shepherd, what did they do? They had recourse to the police, maintaining that they wanted to be reimbursed for what that one had carried off from them. That old woman who had lost her trinkets and also devotional objects was truly inconsolable about it. So great was the quarrel they made of it that for a good while we were tormented by it. One fine day, tired, I went there myself and had to suffer a little; but the fields remained ever more beautiful.

Conversion of a dying sinner.

My voice:

— There is no longer need for you to stay in this field, but others are waiting for you that are in great need.

Without further ado I set out, and I would have wished to find more easily the farmstead to which I was sent.

Along the way two souls draw near to me, black as coal.

My God, these are two demons!

— No! — they answer me — We do not yet belong to them, because the body to which we belong is alive. We have come to warn you and to beg you to obtain our conversion for us; if not, we certainly go to damnation.

— Alas! to whom do you belong?

And at once they answered me.

Horrible fright!

— What can I do?

— Save us!

— Oh! how willingly I would do it! but how?

One of them told me that, if I ran, I would arrive in time, and would certainly save her.

Without heeding anything else, I began to run like a mad dog, and I arrived. Truly: a father of many children — horror! He knew only how to blaspheme! I tried so many things that, repentant, he asked my Lord’s forgiveness and, comforted by the Lord, he expired clasping the Crucifix; and I saw his soul, no longer black, but ashen gray, the sign of a painful purgatory. It was not slow in coming to thank me.

And the other? there was no more hope, and in fact I saw it go down. How ignorant man is! He knows that there is a devil who dwells in hell and who was condemned by God for ever, and they follow him to have the same lot of an eternity of horrible pains; and yet, obstinate, blinded, they will not leave that monster and give themselves to the Lord. Horrible blindness! And yet it is a fact that is seen all too often.

Portrait of the model worker.

Running along this disastrous road, I met the good worker and she, seeing me, told me of many vicissitudes she had gone through: the battles she had fought with certain shepherds who see their own good in a quite curious way.

She is full of spirit and endowed with uncommon courage, especially when she handles the affairs of the fields, and a certain something… She is the mistress of it but, through her great charity and humility, she does not want people to concern themselves with her, but wants to give everything to the Lord in secret; that the Lord God may be the only witness of her actions; for Him alone she likes to work in His vineyard. Her work is just, her aim upright; so her actions are to be admired. The zeal she shows in action is something great, her faith has no limits: she submits everything to the judgment of others, while she is endowed with no little discernment; her energy in working is something… What reigns in that heart cannot be described.

She feels deeply and would not want any human creature ever to suffer, and very willingly she would take upon herself the toils of those who suffer, for whom she bears so much affection. And I can truly assure that she suffers far less in bearing the sufferings of others herself than in knowing or seeing those to whom she bears so much affection suffer.

Oh! creature of so generous a soul, who possesses an inexpressible heart! How much she has relieved me in the midst of horrible anguish! She feels ready to do everything, provided the oppressed is relieved. Her work, in which she is laboring with such zeal and for which her heart is panting to see it completed: how pleasing to the Lord is this great anxiety of hers! And the work is as if she had already finished it; before God it stands so, and for it she has doubled her merit. Blessed are you, who have known so well how to give the treasures to the One who gave them to you, which will certainly be doubled for you!

I thought I was dreaming when I heard myself speaking so well of so noble a creature. Roused from deep recollection, my voice:

— Set out! for it is no longer time to remain in these parts; you must go where for some time now there have been certain farmsteads that are not going well: the workers give little care to their fields, and already the weeds are spreading. If you delay, the harvest will be very scanty. So, courage! for strength will never fail you, and indeed you will find good people there who will help you.

And it stopped.

«I know nothing, but He who sent me knows everything».

Although very tired, and in very rainy weather, I set out on my way. My humanity, averse to ever new sufferings, complained of it and would have liked to find some means of preventing so long a journey; but such was the will of my Master. So it was necessary to obey without remarks.

But the dragon, ready to join forces with my humanity, came and whispered to me insistently:

— Do not move! you will be lost. So true is this that you will bring nothing to those farmsteads but disorder and scandal by your bad conduct.

— How can that be? — I answered that ugly one. — Where are these bad deeds? O ugly monster! withdraw, for you have nothing to do with me. My voice alone is my guide.

But he would not be silent. Tired of hearing him, I turned toward him and gave him a firm command to go away. And so I was freed of him.

Along the way I met a good shepherd. He was off my path but, seeing me, he came up to me and asked me whether the field toward which I was heading was very far. I answered him:

— Very far.

And he:

— But how is it that you intend to walk even by night?

— If it be the will of God, I am ready to do this too.

— That would not be my advice at all, he answered.

— Certainly, — I said to him, — your advice is human and, according to ordinary ways, that is how it ought to be done.

But I answered thus because I saw that my path was always marked out. Since I never paid heed to anything but keeping firmly to my own path, he could not understand this language. He insists, and threatens me that, if I did not stop at his church, I would repent of it and suffer grave misfortunes. And I kept repeating:

— I will do nothing but the will of my Lord.

He stopped near his church and wanted to bar my way.

— No! — I said to him in a resolute tone. — I cannot!

He grew angry and said to me: how could that be? that he would take responsibility for my stopping, since this was the will of God.

— Let me pass, and you may very well stay here!

And I quickly went on ahead. But he remained standing still for some time, as long as he could see me, as if astonished. And every now and then I looked back at him in the distance.

He remained thus for a little while and then caught up with me:

— I cannot rest (thinking) how a creature can have such courage; I had not the heart to turn back, and I think I shall follow you as far as your destination.

I thanked him and said to him:

— God, my Master, will reward you for it, for I have nothing.

Seeing that the night was advancing, he said to me in a resolute tone:

— Let us turn back! Certainly you are completely deceived. Tell me: do you know where you are going, and whether the road we are on is the right one?

— Oh! — I answered him with a smile. — I know nothing, but He who sent me knows everything.

And he:

— Ah! strange indeed! Poor me, whatever have I done? You seem to me a scatterbrain, and your exaltation makes you see as great what can never be.

— A fine reproof indeed! — I answered. — You are quite right, for, reasoning as a man, it cannot be otherwise. For so many years I have served my Master, and never once have I found myself lost; He has always made me run very well.

— Oh! what a head! Your very speech is that of an ignorant creature.

— You are right, — I answered. — I have no other science than the will of my Lord!

And he:

— Come! let us have done with it! I am turning back.

— Go, then: I am not afraid.

My voice:

— You will soon have arrived: ask him to follow you. Laughing, I said to him:

— We are nearly there.

But he:

— So you do know!

— You want to know too much. It is better that we say the prayer to the most holy Virgin and, certainly, when it is finished, we shall find the poor farmstead; and with all their heart the good workers will give you something to refresh yourself and then a little bed to rest on.

— Oh! what a head, what a head! do you know where you are going?

— Where the will of God sends me. Is that enough for you?

And I began the Rosary. And behold, then a little light is seen.

— There! I said. — Look over there!

— Oh! — he said with a deep sigh. — This night was oppressing me: I feel myself reviving. Forgive my too bold words.

At once the good creatures were seen; they made an unequaled celebration. I commended to them that good shepherd, who had remained as if in ecstasy. At once they gave him refreshment, and he could say nothing else but that he had suffered greatly on that journey, but that he was happy to have met creatures so good and all of such extraordinary cheerfulness.

It is a horrible thing to leave the All in order to give oneself to nothing! 110.

But so beautiful a meeting was embittered for me when I saw that one was missing. Alas! where can she be? I go up to one and ask her for news of her. She answers me in a low voice that she always avoids them and is very badly upset. I withdrew, trying to see her, but she was not to be found. My God, where can she be! When I had found her, she would not speak to me at all. She was always gloomy, with her eyes on the ground, her face as sullen as could be. For a long while I tried gentleness with her; when my voice:

— The lash is needed!

Then I raised my voice and ordered her to resolve her problem and to say what she had decided to do. Oh! then the silence was broken: with coarse words she insulted the Work of the Lord, from which she had received so much good.

— Stop, — I said to her, — diabolical tongue! Remember that up to this very day you have lived on nothing but the bread of God!

Seeing that she could say nothing but: I want to go elsewhere! I said to her:

— But it is not so, wretched creature! A wolf awaits you: take good care not to let yourself be devoured! It is a horrible thing to leave the All in order to give oneself to nothing!»

At these words she began to think. I went on:

— Yes, think seriously whom you are betraying and listen to the voice of your conscience; abandon your troubled ways and return to the fold, where the dear Master awaits you to embrace you again.

She believed that I knew everything; instead, I was repeating what I heard my voice tell me. She stood perplexed, and looked now here, now there, to see whether she could see or hear anyone. I began to speak again:

— Heart of mud, putrid conscience! away with that anxiety of yours! and once and for all break this chain, which leads you to nothing but despair!

She looks at me, stops, and weeps. O most loving Master! You have won! The steel has broken! Yes! Coming close to me, she clasps my hand.

— Yes! — she too repeats; and afterwards:

— Who are you, that one cannot resist your words?

— O dear creature! I am, as you well know, the poor slave of my Master, and yours too: it is He who was working in your heart with His grace; I could say nothing; He alone worked in you.

— Oh! I want to belong wholly to my Master, — she said; and she took off certain objects and papers, and gave them all to me. — I want nothing but my God!

Oh! great moment, sweet Love!

— Yes, wholly for Him alone, dear creature! Come with me, let us leave this field and go where you will work without fears: God, and creatures for love of Him!

My voice:

— Make haste to leave in all speed!

— Come, let us go!

But the enemy puts it into her mind that first she wants to settle many matters. I kept repeating to her:

— Let us go! Others whom we shall send will settle everything.

But no: she grew ever more determined to want to put things in order. At last she answers me:

— What are you afraid of? Did I not strip myself of everything and, with a solemn declaration, consecrate myself wholly to my Lord?

I saw that malicious serpent buzzing around her, whispering to her to stay put. Oh! without heeding anything else, I ordered that ugly one to withdraw. Astonished, she watched what I was doing with such severity and said to me:

— Whom are you speaking to?

I answered her nothing. And she:

— Forgive me!

— Well, then, are you coming?

— Yes! — she answered. — I am ready.

In fact, the ugly one had gone away. She had lost that firmness, or rather, her pride, when she said (that she could not go away) leaving things in poor order. Everything vanished from her mind, and we set out on our way.

God wants love more than work — The value of prayer in desolation.

From afar a trampling of horses is heard. The worker takes fright and takes me by the hand:

— I am afraid, alas!

— We must fear nothing: God is with us and for us; no harm can come to us.

— But… — she — Perhaps I?…

And she begins to scream. Oh! what can it be? I clasp her hand:

— How do you forget your promises so soon? O poor heart! It needs to be thoroughly cleansed of the mud that is still there. Courage! Those approaching are good people, who care about nothing: they think only of themselves.

So it happened. As they drew near, with a gracious greeting they bade us good day. She was set at peace, and wanted at all costs to know how I knew who those people were. Then I answered her:

— But only a moment ago I told you: we must fear nothing, for we have God with us.

And I began to speak of my Master, telling her that it was for Him she worked; but it was evident that she did not know Him. She remained enchanted.

— What? — I said to her. — So much work, and then you do not know at all the Master, the Teacher, our Lord, His riches, His treasures? O poor creature!

And eagerly she said to me:

— Tell me, for charity’s sake! I feel myself wholly changed. It seemed to me that I truly loved Him; yes, I served Him, but I did not love Him and felt nothing for Him; only that I had to serve Him!

— Ah no! He wants to be loved, and more than work He wants love. Martha, Martha! — said our Teacher — you are too anxious! While Magdalene felt greatly that she loved Him and gave herself wholly to love, reckoning work less (cf. Lk 10:38-42). So must we do, for work must never be in excess of prayer, because only by praying and meditating on the Passion of our divine Teacher do we learn to know Him and to love Him much. Prayer obtains a great deal; it is necessary above all when we are in aridity, and also when temptation troubles us, filling us with weariness in prayer: it is then that we must make an effort to succeed in completing all our prayers.

The effort that must be made renders our prayer more acceptable to God than when we find in it relief, recollection and union with God. The satisfaction of feeling that consolation in prayer God permits to beginners, so that they may become attached to that delight and may thereby go forward, but without making progress; whereas those who pray without delight, without consolations, whom faith alone guides and assures, walk along the way of perfection and take giant strides.

She listened to me attentively and every now and then interrupted me to ask for explanations. Kindled with fervor and full of that enthusiasm, what would this creature not have done! But I restrained her; only one thing I left her in her fervor: to strive so that she too might come to obtain (so great a good). She surprised me by saying to me:

— Shall I come to obtain this without thinking of anything else?

— Yes! — I answered her — provided that you hold firmly to your fervor.

She, happy, gave herself wholly to denying herself in order to be wholly God’s. And I left her.

The judgments of God are inscrutable.

While I would have wished to rest, behold, the hour strikes for me to go to work. And where shall I begin? Without noticing it, I found myself at the far end of a dark room. A voice could be heard from which, in a very stifled way, a sad lament came forth.

I drew near. My God! a soul who had disappeared many years ago and had gone to join the majority; and yet her daughter, who some ten years after the mother was passing through there. The daughter said nothing to me. She was still very well dressed in ash-gray, but she showed me that she no longer suffered and that little was lacking for her to enter the heavenly homeland. I say little, but it is always a great deal.

But her poor mother was suffering greatly and was lamenting so that I ran to help her. She lay thrown upon a board and was suffocating horribly. She was asking me for help, calling me by name. Oh! how was this? The daughter came close to me and said to me:

— I can do nothing! I beg you to help my mother. I wanted to raise her up, but she has received barely a little relief from it.

I assured her that I would do all I could so that God might relieve her from so painful a state. A mystery! In a flash everything is explained to me, and I thought: how is it that a saint, for whose beatification this lady spent no small amount of money, nevertheless leaves her in such pains?

The justice of God is terrible; His words imprinted in the holy Gospel are unchangeable. Everything is infinitely just; His purposes are inscrutable. Yes, my Lord! I adore them, and I observe that everything in You is thus infinite, my Lord. Your yoke is sweet (cf. Mt 11:30); the pains that are felt in it are so many delights that raise us up to the contemplation of Your greatness. The smaller I feel myself to be, the more I find that I possess the sight to see Your greatness and infinite Majesty; most perfect are Your words: Whoever wishes to become great, let him strive to make himself small (cf. Mt 18:4).

The Virgin Mary protects her from the brigands.

A continual running, although worn out by labors and sufferings. I would have wished to stop for a little in order to rest and find relief. My voice:

— Do not heed human demands, but only the will of your Teacher!

Having heard this, I set out on the journey, running without knowing where, or what might happen to me. Having set out on the way, without a bag, I held only the Sorrowful Virgin clasped in my hands, and went along reciting her Sorrows.

What happened to me? In the dark of night I came upon a stranger. He joined me in walking; he said nothing, only every now and then he seemed annoyed. Oh! what fear! Alone! my God, so alone! Ah! send me my angel to help me: I am dying of fright!

We were on a bridge and, at the murmur of the water that ran strongly, I grew greatly agitated. I clasped that image and begged her for her help. And he stood motionless in front of me, at a distance of a single step. At last I see a small little light: running, I found myself near it. Ah! what agitation! It was a small lamp burning beside an image of the most holy Virgin. How many things I said to her in a moment!

But he did not allow me to stop. I say «allow» because, since this was under a small vault, I feared that he too would stop and say something to me. So I tried more and more to walk on.

O most holy Virgin! wherever am I? Behold, a trampling of horses; a voice says:

— We are in the city!

Oh! he vanished, that is, he went away. A few steps further on I found myself in a hospital where our workers were caring for those poor unfortunates. What a surprise at seeing me! how they all raised their voices, marveling at how I had arrived there. They crowded me with questions: how had I been able, at that hour, to be spared so terrible a misfortune! All the people who ran to that place to see me were all marveling greatly; and I stood there as if enchanted. At last I said:

— Why do you ask me so many questions? whatever could have happened to me?

They answered:

— These parts are full of evildoers and nemo dares to move except with a large escort of armed men. Terrible things happen, and one always hears of massacres and every sort of wickedness. No one comes out of there alive.

Oh! how was this? And then I told them about the one who had frightened me so much, but who never dared to say a word to me. They wanted a thousand particulars.

— But he wore a hat pulled so far over his face that it was impossible to see him.

— He was certainly a brigand! — they said — and you have remained alive!

Oh! how I felt within me a violent upheaval! I felt myself trembling all over, but I did not want anyone to notice my agitation. I asked, for charity’s sake, to be accompanied to where my God was in their little oratory; and, prostrate on the ground, I thanked my God and the most holy Virgin for the grace received.

Returning the next day, I was escorted by armed men, as badly as I had spent the night, working together with the dear custodians beside the sick and after having settled all that my Master wished. On seeing myself followed, or rather accompanied, by those bearded fellows, I felt a kind of inner distress so that my strength failed me.

A lesson to the workers without faith.

Outside the town, I entered the vast field.

[…]. 111.

My way was always prepared for new torments. When I believed I was a little at peace and able to work together with the others, behold, my voice commands me to go elsewhere. There were certain people near our farmstead, in a large field, who, through their little confidence in God, were in despair, because they feared that their provisions would fail them.

— Why, creatures of little faith, do you despair so? — I said to them.

They looked at me. And then they answered me:

— How can we not be so, when our future is clearly seen? We lack everything; and more than anything else it is seeing ourselves deprived of human help. And then, — they added, — how did you manage to come?

I answered them:

— God, my dear Master, is the one who sent me.

But they took little account of my words and went on grumbling and looking at me with an indifference beyond belief. They looked me up and down, perhaps to see whether I had brought them anything. Seeing them thus, I took my leave; but they, cold as ice, barely gave me a greeting, and nothing more!

Running with all the strength I had, I went to certain good people, whose heart was full of charity and, having asked them for alms for the poor workers, I received them in great quantity. I kissed that ground and with joined hands thanked the benefactress.

I set out to return to those without faith, whom I had left numb with the cold of the soul, brutalized by their not very good conduct, letting go untilled a most beautiful field that the dear Teacher had given them to cultivate; but they had little desire to work. I met a charming peasant girl; she stopped me and, calling me by name, handed me the basket, telling me that her mistress had told her to bring it to me.

— Who is your mistress? — I asked her.

— I am forbidden to say, — she answered me. I took this basket, which was very large, and gave it to a little boy to carry for me, because I had not enough strength to carry all that I had gathered. When I arrived at the farmstead, the welcome was no longer cold; on the contrary, they would have liked to gild me.

10 December 1893.

XV

Always ready for sacrifice under the yoke of work.

(9 March 1894 a. P.

When I believed I had traveled through enough valleys and crags and rivers and sea, overcome by extreme weakness, leaning against a tree trunk which I believed strong, I stopped, sure of recovering my strength. The trunk weakens, collapses; I see it giving way beneath me. An agitation invades me; at every moment I see myself plunged into the abyss. Where am I to save myself? Turning to the wonder-worker of Paola 112 for help, I prayed to him earnestly: he was of bronze! Turning to another protectress of mine, with bitter weeping, I sent her supplications that she might save me. She answered me in a firm tone:

— I have seen to it.

But meanwhile the trunk was crumbling more and more; to all appearances it was no longer possible to hope for the slightest support from it. Screaming, I called my angel. I am lost! What I saw was frightening to me. And weeping I clung to the foot of the cross, while my strength was reduced to its lowest point. My angel seized me by one arm and, shaking me out of so dreadful a lethargy, gave me strength and, pointing out to me a long and sorrowful way that awaited me, said to me:

— Go! God sends you there: you will have much to suffer, but you will be upheld by the strength of the Lord.

I looked at him and, weeping, said to him:

— Ah! promise me that you will always be with me.

And he:

— Am I not always near you?

— No! — I said to him.

And he, still smiling at me:

— I will be with you, do not fear! The dragon will not stir from beneath my foot. You will have to struggle with every sort of people; they will try to stop you on the way, and even those who are with you will urge you to turn back. Woe to you if you heed the human claws that will be raised against you to intimidate you.

I look at the way and feel myself invaded by a horrible terror; as in a flash my mind is struck with dread. My angel notices this agitation of mine and in a severe tone says to me:

— Think of fulfilling the will of God: woe to you if you turn back!

And he vanished.

Mute, my forehead resting on my hand, I stayed motionless. After a long while I began again:

— Where is the strength, my Crucified One, to do what You command me? This poor slave of Yours is always ready for sacrifice under the yoke of work: she will never dare to stop! (Your orders) shall be carried out!

Always onward, without ever stopping, in spite of the dictates of human prudence.

Contrary to the expectation of all the workers, I set out on my way, and at the first farmstead where I stopped, after a long journey, I began to have great struggles, for numberless were the people who tried to dissuade me, pointing out to me that this road was entrenched with evildoers; they tried to tell me every sort of frightening tale. But no! I clung to the feet of my Crucified One and asked Him what I was to do.

— Onward! — He answered me. — Do not fear! So I arrived at another farmstead. The snow was falling in large flakes, the cold was something horrible; those great valleys and the very high mountains were all covered with snow. Every so often, a poor man with a donkey, who helped each other, I would say, in turn, for now one fell and now the other: they were trying to approach certain farmhouses that could barely be made out, being covered with snow. It was picturesque!

After having traveled many leagues, whenever I came upon anyone, they at once urged me to turn back, because that road was most dangerous and it was not fitting for a creature to venture along it; and when they saw my obstinacy, they tried to lead astray the workers who were with me. Having arrived at a certain point, I truly did see certain evildoers who were preparing to start a fight, and it was clear that they had a great desire for blood. Seized with fright, a thousand thoughts crossed my mind: the fear that the workers I had with me might fail me out of fright, and all that a mind disturbed by such horrible events witnessed, and by fancies, can create. I felt like stopping. I began to pray:

— My Master! must I stop? How can it be that this is Your will: that I should go further forward, while with every step I advance the evildoers increase? Oh! shall I stop?

As I was saying this, a dear soul of mine, who dwells in the heavenly homeland, appeared and said to me:

— Do not fear: onward! Nothing untoward will happen to you. I will always be with you.

Full of vigor, encouraged by so great a saint, I ran swiftly along my path and, crossing very many fields and sea, at last I arrived happily where my Lord had ordered me.

How can I express the joy of the workers who came to meet me? Among the many there was one who stood out in a singular way (in her appearance). Who was she? A great lady who for years has been working in the fields of the Lord in an extraordinary way: my beloved one, untiring for the greater glory of God. She, endowed with a sublime spirit, as always was a great relief to me in everything! Like a matron, distinguished by her noble qualities, she always preserves so charitable a heart and an upright and sincere spirit. Oh! sublime woman, who think only of relieving the wretched! This slave, generously benefited by you, beholds your merits and your great virtues. Great knowledge God gave you! 113.

Symbolic vision of the suffering Church: My God, accept me as a victim!

Sorrowfully I went on my way, seized by the thought that on this earth nothing was worthy of a God. Why this profound thought? Is it not You, O Creator, who were pleased to create all that exists?

I raise my eyes to heaven: what do I see? Seven tablets reddening with blood, which seemed to be held up by streaks of fire; a most beautiful angel, very like Saint Michael, held them up with a long vine-shoot. In the distance, Peter, head of the Church, who was praying, grew gloomy looking at the tablets, and wept. A legion of angels, who were singing a sorrowful chant, accompanied it with their instruments. Everything was sorrowful.

All stop. In a great and infinite space, almost dark, beautiful souls clothed in mourning could be seen. Here and there black hangings could be seen. An infinity of people: they stood indifferent, as if they were capable of understanding nothing. Every now and then a loud groan came forth: from where? — I said to myself — I look at Saint Peter: it was not he who was sending forth such a lament: no! What a lament! it was heart-rending. I asked the angel to explain to me what it meant. He answered me:

— It is the Church that suffers!

— The tablets that you hold up, what do they mean?

— I cannot tell you.

He showed me a horrible thing, and said to me:

— This is a most acute sorrow that the Church suffers.

At that sight I felt myself dying: such was the terror of it. It was the indifference of Catholics! It seemed that each one was driving sharp daggers, as it were, into a Heart. How can this be repaired? My God! accept this slave of Yours, who offers herself as a victim in reparation! I felt nothing. Turning to the angel, I said to him:

— Ah! take this sight away from me and obtain that God may accept me as a victim of expiation.

I would have wished to make reparation for everything, but I could no longer bear such a sight. Mercy, my God! I saw nothing more: only the tablets and the angel.

— Tell me, what do they mean? They were becoming ever redder with blood. The angel gave me a look, and everything vanished. 114.

The speech of the angel of God is very different from that of the infernal «boarders».

So exhausted, I fell asleep sitting on a stone; another, larger one lay nearby and served me as a pillow. So fixed in my mind was what I had seen, and the tablets! In my sleep I heard an angel (a false one); he was telling me that he would explain it to me, that if he had not told me it was because he did not wish to satisfy my curiosity. Meanwhile he told me nothing.

When I awoke, this great pretender was near me. I said to him:

— Why do you tell me nothing?

— First you must do certain things that I will tell you, and so you will know better the secrets of God.

I look at him, saying to him:

— Who are you!

— What? do you doubt that I am an angel sent (by God)?

And he wanted to persuade me of many things with events that were to happen. I rose imperiously to go away. He stopped me, stepping in front of me:

— No, stop! Listen to me, — he said to me — otherwise you will regret it.

And I:

— Your speech is not good: you are a boarder of darkness.

He looked at me: he was very handsome, but I saw clearly that he was a demon.

— Leave me and go away!

He answered:

— You will regret it! Let me come and accompany you, for so I will defend you from certain snakes that are along the way.

— No! — I said to him in a resolute tone. — Away, away, infernal monster!

He became furious and said:

— So many souls I hold bound by this deceit of mine: you alone have recognized me.

— Away! I do not want to hear you.

— Listen to me: I want to tell you how many souls I hold under my direction.

— Away! Tell me, who are they?

— Oh! that, never!

And he sneered at me and kept coming along behind me.

I grasped my Crucifix and said:

— Stop, horrible monster!

He remained motionless.

My voice:

— Send him to his chains!

So I commanded him. And he went away.

I went on thinking of the souls he deludes. It is true, alas — I said — and they are so attached that, if their guide exhorts them to drive him away and not to listen to him, they suffer from it and give little credence to their guide. How much harm he does to their souls! He distils into their hearts a subtle pride, which can hardly be drawn out of them. They are irascible. Oh! how many other faults they commit because he suggests them, and makes them believe an infinity of them.

But very different is the speech of the angel of God from that of the infernal boarders. There are too many of them in this century; they seem to divine things, but how many they get wrong! and then how do they end?

Apparition of a soul in purgatory.

While I was reasoning thus, there came before me a soul whom I could not make out. I asked her what she wanted: she answered me nothing. I signed my forehead with the sign of the cross: nothing!

— In the name of God, speak!

Nothing! What distress! She was so wrapped in a black mantle that she did not let me see her face. Seeing that she did not answer, I grasped my Crucifix and ordered her to speak or to go away. Could this be a monster? or someone who is pretending in this way? And then, in reality, could it be a man?

My mind grows confused, my legs and feet waver, I can no longer walk. And that black, wrapped figure kept coming nearer and nearer.

— Away, now! I tell you to go: return to your chains!

Nothing! At last I began to pray, and then this poor soul made me a sign, showing me what she held in her hand. A horrible sight! She wanted, alas, to make me understand what she had done in life. At that sight I grieved over it and prayed for her.

My God! Your justice, well deserved by our souls, makes us understand with what contempt we, miserable creatures, have treated Your most holy Passion. But this slave of Yours gathers up Your most precious blood and offers it to the eternal Father in expiation of the pains and torments of these souls, that they may be set free, or that it may relieve them for a single instant from such cruel sufferings». 115.

notes.travagli-en-fn109: A new omission in the 1897 edition. The Foundress continues to suffer and to hope for a happy solution.
notes.travagli-en-fn112: Saint Francis of Paola, founder of the Minims, one of the patron saints of the Servant of God.
notes.travagli-en-fn115: The tale remains broken off, without a conclusion, as if to indicate that the story remains open, waiting for the Voice to make itself heard, imperious and comforting, as so many times before: Onward! you still have a long way to go!
notes.travagli-en-fn111: Yet one last omission in the Palermo edition, for the reason mentioned above.
notes.travagli-en-fn113: The interpretation of the metaphors does not seem difficult: the end of so troubled a journey, across fields and «sea», is Palermo; the noblewoman, «my beloved one», can be none other than the Princess of Fitalia.
notes.travagli-en-fn114: Once again the theme of the sufferings of the Church, with the desire to offer herself as a «victim of expiation». On Good Friday 1885, while she was sharing experientially in the torments of Christ’s Passion, she received light on the continuation of that same Passion in the Mystical Body: «O my Love! what is this that I feel? — They are the pains that the Church suffers!» (Mem. V, 3, p. 74 f. See above, note 76).
notes.travagli-en-fn110: Rosa Gattorno, like other great mystics, loves to designate God as «my All», contrasting it with her own «nothing». Cf. Fisionomia spirituale, pp. 70, 104, 163, 178, 196, 274.
